title: Strict cosimplicial injective replacements and alternating-total comparison
statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a Grothendieck abelian category [def-sp-grothendieck-abelian], and write $\operatorname{Ch}^{\ge0}(\mathcal A)$ for nonnegative cochain complexes, extended by zero in negative degrees [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Let $\Delta$ be the category of finite nonempty ordered sets $[n]$ and order-preserving maps. For a strict diagram $C:\Delta\to\operatorname{Ch}^{\ge0}(\mathcal A)$ define $T(C)^r=\bigoplus_{n+q=r}C_n^q$ and $d_T=\delta+(-1)^n d_C$, with $\delta=\sum_i(-1)^iC(d^i)$ [def-sp-double-complex-total]. There are a functor $I$ on nonnegative complexes and a natural quasi-isomorphism $\eta:\mathrm{id}\to I$, with all terms of $I(A)$ injective [def-sp-injective-resolutions], such that $R(C)=I\circ C$ and $u_C=(\eta_{C_n})_n$ define a strict functorial replacement of cosimplicial complexes and $T(u_C):T(C)\to T(R(C))$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Here $I\circ C$ denotes postcomposition by $I$. Every strict map $f:C\to D$ has the strict lift $R(f)_n=I(f_n)$ with $R(f)u_C=u_Df$, and the same $I$ and $\eta$ apply to whole strictly augmented diagrams, including their nonnegative augmentation objects. More generally, any strict map $v:C\to D$ whose every $v_n$ is a quasi-isomorphism induces a quasi-isomorphism $T(v)$. The sign maps $(-1)^{nq}$ on $C_n^q$ specify natural chain isomorphisms from the total of the transposed double complex $(C_n^q,d_C,\delta)$, indexed by $(q,n)$, to $T(C)$.

proof.text: By the Grothendieck functorial embedding theorem choose functorial injective embeddings in $\mathcal A$. Apply the lower-bound-preserving complex-resolution theorem to obtain one functor $I$ and natural quasi-isomorphism $\eta$. Restrict its domain and codomain to complexes zero below $0$: the theorem preserves that bound, and every term remains injective. Equivalently restrict to nonnegative indices and extend by zero; maps in negative degrees are uniquely zero, so these operations identify the complex categories.

proof.text: For every $\alpha:[n]\to[m]$ set $R(C)(\alpha)=I(C(\alpha))$. The identity and composition laws follow directly from those of $I$ and $C$. For $f:C\to D$, naturality follows from $I(D(\alpha))I(f_n)=I(f_m)I(C(\alpha))$; hence $R(f)_n=I(f_n)$ defines a strict map. Naturality of $\eta$ gives $I(f_n)\eta_{C_n}=\eta_{D_n}f_n$ and the same equation for every simplex operator. These equations also apply to all augmentation arrows after adjoining $[-1]$; use $I$ on the nonnegative augmentation complex too. Thus replacements of whole augmented diagrams and maps are strict and functorial.

For any $C$ form the transposed bicomplex $B(C)^{q,n}=C_n^q$ with first differential $d_C$ and second differential $\delta$. In $\delta^2$, pair the coface composite $d^j d^i$ with $d^i d^{j-1}$ for $i<j$; their signs $(-1)^{i+j}$ and $(-1)^{i+j-1}$ cancel. Every composite occurs once in such a pair. Each coface is a chain map, so $d_C\delta=\delta d_C$. Thus this is a first-quadrant double complex. Its total differential is $d_C+(-1)^q\delta$. All diagonals are finite. A strict diagram map $v$ commutes with both differentials, so it induces $B(v)$ and its total map.

source.place: Tag 012X, section-double-complex; coface cancellation written out

proof.text: Define $S_C:\operatorname{Tot}(B(C))\to T(C)$ on the $(q,n)$ summand by $(-1)^{nq}$. For the $d_C$ component, $S_Cd_C$ has sign $(-1)^{n(q+1)}$, equal to the sign $(-1)^{nq+n}$ in $d_TS_C$. For the $\delta$ component, $S_C(-1)^q\delta$ has sign $(-1)^{q+(n+1)q}=(-1)^{nq}$, again equal to that in $d_TS_C$. Thus $S_C$ is a chain map. Its inverse has the same summand signs since $(-1)^{2nq}=1$. For every $v$, scalar multiplication commutes with $v_n^q$, giving $S_D\operatorname{Tot}(B(v))=T(v)S_C$. This proves precisely the asserted natural sign isomorphism.

If each $v_n$ is a quasi-isomorphism, apply first-quadrant column comparison to $B(v)$. With the indices chosen above, $B(C).\mathrm{flip}.X\,n$ is exactly the complex $C_n$ in degree $q$, so every comparison hypothesis is the given one. Hence $\operatorname{Tot}(B(v))$ is a quasi-isomorphism. The natural isomorphisms $S_C,S_D$ identify its cohomology maps with those of $T(v)$, which are therefore isomorphisms. In particular set $D=R(C)$ and $v=u_C$; every component is $\eta_{C_n}$ from step 1. This gives $T(u_C)$ and the general assertion.
